newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar - Japan's Nisso Iwai seeks Cuba freight.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - Japan's Nisso Iwai seeks Cuba freight.

text.p: Japan's Nissho Iwai Corp confirmed on Wednesday it was in the freight market for Cuban sugar, quoting for 24,000 to 25,000 tonnes to Japan for full January dates.
"Yes, we're in the market. We're seeking the freight from Cuba as quick as possible during January," a Nissho Iwai official said. He did not give details.
Japanese traders said they were gradually buying for April-June delivery but activity was slow.
Indonesia's sugar buying was slowing down as most of the nation's purchasing had been completed, said a source at an international firm's Hong Kong office.
"They may buy a little bit more after January 1, but it's mostly over," he said.
Thai sugar traders were said reluctant to sell sugar, put off by a soft market, other sugar sources in Hong Kong said.
Some Japanese traders said that sugar crushing in Thailand had been delayed, but the details could not be confirmed.
Premiums for January/March delivery were quoted at 0.85/0.85 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB basis, against 0.80/0.90 cents a week ago.
March/May and May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.46/0.48 cents and 0.49/0.50 cents on the New York exchange, they said.
Premiums for Thai raw sugar this week remained bearish, partly due to International Sugar Organisation (ISO) estimates about a higher sugar surplus, Japanese traders in Tokyo said.
"Thai premiums are slightly weaker against last week. The ISO's revised sugar surplus figure helped accelerate the bearish sentiment," a sugar trader at a major Tokyo trade house said.
The ISO earlier this week estimated the world sugar surplus for 1996/97 at three million tonnes, against its previous estimate of 2.5 million tonnes.
A sugar trader at a large Hong Kong firm said China's demand for fine crystal sugar had increased in the past two months.
"We have received many enquiries from traders wanting to sell fine crystal sugar into China," he said.

China's demand for fine crystal sugar would likely keep increasing as consumers' tastes became more sophisticated and incomes grew, the trader said, noting he had seen bags of South Korean fine crystal sugar even in remote grocery stores.
Meanwhile, prices of beet sugar in northern China had equalised with southern Chinese prices, and were both around 4,200 yuan ($506) per tonne, traders in the British colony said.
Prices in Guangxi, China's southern sugar-producing area, were around 4,000 yuan ($481) per tonne, Hong Kong traders said.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
